chapter_theme: The narrator finishes the head-to-foot portrait of Vijayai, princess of Videham, which King Sachchandan paints in his heart and carries away; he sends his suit to her father, the elders and ministers give her to him, and the chapter dwells on the couple's mutual, all-absorbing pleasure, the delight that the next verses will name as the king's slipping from the guard of his land.

cast.role: princess of Videham, Sachchandan's queen and Civakan's mother
Vijayai's mothers, elder sisters and elders who give her in marriage

174.reading: The narrator's head-to-foot portrait of the princess reaches her thighs: they shame an elephant's trunk, are round as a plantain stem, soft as cotton dyed with lac, and wear a jewelled girdle clasp shaped like a makara.
174.nuance: The catalogue begun in 163 is the narrator's, offered before the king sees her; its excess is the point, since the next verses make this description the image the king paints in his heart.

175.reading: Her knees are praised as smooth, rounded and closely jointed, with a beauty the narrator says no human has.
175.nuance: Line 1 (கவிழிய வாய் மேல் பிறங்காப் பாண்டிலா) is hard to construe; the reading of the knee-cap image is a guess. மக்களுக்கு இல்லாத says outright that the beauty is more than human, preparing the king's taking her for an அணங்கு in 181.

176.reading: Her calves are neither too fleshy nor too thin, hairless and of just measure, rounded like a smooth stalk.
176.nuance: The beauty praised is one of right proportion (நீடாது குறுகாது நிகர் அமைந்த அளவின): the ideal is measure, not abundance. Line 3 (சேடு ஆவ நாழிகையின்) is obscure.

177.reading: Her pair of feet, ringing with gold anklets, foot-ornaments and pearl-filled சிலம்பு, are curved like a young tortoise's back, and those who praise them find their senses fail.
177.nuance: The last line turns the praise back on the praiser: feeling sinks (உணர்வு மடிந்து ஒழியும்) in those who praise her feet, a first sign that this beauty disables judgment.

178.reading: Her toes, with nails like the inner petals of the red water-lily, taper, close together and wear gold rings, so lovely that bees swarm to them.

179.reading: Her small soles, as soft as pressed silk-cotton blossom and as if without bone or sinew, rest on the earth so tenderly that a walk of nine spans feels to her like a league.
179.nuance: என்பொடு நரம்பு இன்றி denies the body its frame: the epic's praise works by imagining the beloved's body free of the very bone and sinew that the ascetic verses make the whole of it.

180.reading: The king painted this form on the cloth of his heart with the brush of thought, gave it eyes with his own gaze, sprinkled it with the water of love and strewed it with the endless flowers of desire.
180.nuance: The whole catalogue of 163 to 179 is retold as the king's own act of painting: what the narrator described is now the image desire makes, and the verb சிதறினான் (scattered) closes on excess, not on choice.
180.event: Sachchandan fixes the princess's image in his heart and gives himself to desire for her.

181.reading: Caught in the net of the long eyes of the girl whose lisping mouth has sounds without full letters, Sachchandan, taking her without doubt for a goddess, keeps her in his heart and goes on his way, the king with the bellowing elephant and the bee-hummed garland.
181.nuance: ஐயுறான் அணங்கு எனவே can be read 'not doubting that she is a goddess' or, with the negative taken loosely, 'wondering whether she is a goddess'; the reading changes whether the king is certain or perplexed. அணங்கு also names a being that afflicts, and the king's later ruin makes the double sense apt.
181.event: Sachchandan, snared by the princess's eyes, carries away her image without speaking of it.

182.reading: The garlanded girl is the daughter of the lord who drives elephants that wear bee-swarms for face-cloths, and the name she has won by surpassing all women's beauty is Vijayai.
182.nuance: The name is held back until the portrait is done, and glossed by her beauty: விசயை (Vijaya, victory) is a name earned by surpassing other women (பெண்டிர் தம் பெரு நலம் கடந்து).

183.reading: She dwells in the palace of her father, the lord of the white parasol, as if she were Tirumakal, the goddess of fortune who stands on the golden lotus.
183.nuance: Tirumakal here is praise of a princess; the same goddess will be named as fortune that silently leaves Sachchandan once he is lost in Vijayai (232).

184.reading: Her mothers and elder sisters bow to her anklet-ringed feet as she walks; she is like a right-whorled conch circled by a lesser conch, and like a creeper that bears the honour of her line.
184.nuance: The image of the வலம்புரி among the சலஞ்சலம் makes her the rare and auspicious one among her kin; குலம் புரிந்து அனையது ஓர் கொடி may mean that her family's whole worth has taken the form of a creeper.
184.event: Vijayai's mothers and elder sisters honour her as she walks among them.

185.reading: As her breasts swell and her lightning-thin waist grows thinner, the girl's beauty ripens into womanhood.

186.reading: The king of the great army and rutting elephants, already spoken of, sent his word to the father of the girl.
186.nuance: The narrator steps forward (முந்து நாம் கூறிய) to tie the king of 157 to 161 to this suit. The desire of 180 and 181 turns at once into a formal proposal through her father, the proper road of marriage.
186.event: Sachchandan sends a proposal of marriage to Vijayai's father.

187.reading: Seeing the son-in-law's strength, the maiden's flourishing and the course the wise ministers had weighed, those who judged that the two were fit to be joined gave the doe-like girl to the great king.
187.nuance: கலத்தல் பான்மையில் may mean only 'in the way fit for joining' or 'by the destiny that they should join'; பான்மை means a destined portion in 215, where Sachchandan's fall is said to sprout from it, so the marriage and the ruin may share one cause. The claim is recorded with that doubt. The match is reasoned as well as fated: the ministers' சூழ்ச்சி is named beside it.
187.event: Vijayai's elders and the ministers approve the match, and she is given in marriage to Sachchandan.

claims.claim: a marriage comes about when the couple's apportioned portion is for joining

188.reading: The golden creeper like nectar and the man like a high gold mountain, wounded by Kama's arrows that would not let them go, were united as no other pair anywhere, as the three-eyed god of the angry bull and his goddess are joined.
188.nuance: A Jain epic compares its royal couple to Siva and his consort as plain praise; within twenty verses a counsellor will cite Siva's sharing his body with the mountain king's daughter as a great blame (208).
188.event: Sachchandan and Vijayai are married and united.

189.reading: In their love they were like the radiant couples of the land of pleasure, in their wedded delight like mating serpents, in swelling tenderness like swans, and in their blameless sporting like the wealth of the wild cow.
189.nuance: காம பூமி is the Jain cosmology's land of enjoyment, where couples are born together and live in pleasure without labour; the comparison sets the couple outside the world of work and rule. Line 4's ஆமான் செல்வம் is obscure, and மாசுணம் may name a large serpent.

190.reading: When the loving king and the woman were wed, the glorious king drank her as nectar, and she in turn drank the jewelled king like wine prepared for spear-eyed women.
190.nuance: The verse makes the delight mutual: each drinks the other, he as nectar (அமிர்தம்), she as intoxicating மது. The image of drinking returns in 199, where the drinking goes on while fortune slips.

191.reading: The spear-bearing king, who drank her coral mouth and broad hips, was like a tusker at its fodder, his beloved like sugarcane; she was a lotus and he a shining-winged bee.

192.reading: She, with the grace of a coral doll in a crystal chamber and wide red-cornered eyes like fighting carp, was like a ripe fruit of love, and the king who tasted it tenderly was like a fair-winged bird.
192.nuance: The eyes as fighting carp (களிக் கயல் பொருவ) are a stock praise; the Naladiyar's renunciant names the same carp as the image he refuses (naladiyar:44).

193.reading: Amid heaped flower wreaths, crowns, scented powder, garlands, sandal paste, delicacies of every land, aloe smoke and musk, the great pair lived as if bound to the earth that bears them.
193.nuance: பெறு நிலம் பிணித்திட is unclear: it may say the riches of every land were gathered to them, or that pleasure held them fast to the ground.

194.reading: The joy of their touch, with her bee-sipped garland and dark hair, the anklet on her foot, the ringing girdle and the look of her flowering eyes, was hard to exhaust.
194.nuance: Sound (சிலம்பு, அரவ மேகலை), scent (சுரும்பு உண் கோதை), sight (நோக்கம்) and touch (ஊறு) are gathered in one sentence, with taste in the mouth-drinking of 191 and 196: the senses are all fed from one source.

195.reading: The king of the blood-red spear lingered with his creeper of a wife, with her jewelled young breasts, thin waist and flower-laden hair, as the monsoon cloud lingers in the rain.
195.nuance: வைகும் (lingers, stays) is the hinge: the cloud that stays is the king who stays, and the next verses (198) say what he leaves unguarded while he does.
195.event: Sachchandan stays on with Vijayai, given over to pleasure.

196.reading: Drinking the nectar of her coral lips, resting at her breasts, losing themselves like thunder and lightning, the intimacy of the new marriage was greater than any sea.
196.nuance: கடி மணக் கிழமை, the closeness of the wedding season, is measured by a sea: boundless, and so without a shore to return from.

197.reading: Vijayai, the creeper of love, dwells like an incomparable doll, while maids hold up camphor betel in jewelled caskets and she spits out the red of the chewed leaf.
197.nuance: காமவல்லி names her as love's own creeper; the chapter closes on her as a doll (பாவை), still and adorned, the object of the pleasure that will cost the realm.

links.note: Both are the man's first sight of the woman and both reach for அணங்கு; the Kural's lover wavers among goddess, peahen and woman, while Sachchandan, on the likelier reading, takes her for an அணங்கு without doubt (ஐயுறான்).
links.teaches: The Kural's perplexity at first sight is a lover's healthy doubt; the epic gives a king who does not doubt, and his certainty that she is more than human is the first step of the absorption that later costs him his kingdom.

gains.a: the king's untroubled certainty is seen as a departure from the expected first-sight wavering, marking his surrender as complete
gains.b: the couplet's three-way doubt is shown to hold a check that a man without it, a king, loses

links.note: The Kural's lover says all five senses find their objects in one woman; verse 194 gathers sound, scent, sight and touch in Vijayai and calls the joy inexhaustible.
links.teaches: What the Kural states as the joy of union, with no cost named, the epic puts in a king, and four verses later shows the cost: a man whose senses are all fed from one source slips from guarding the land (198).

gains.a: the sense catalogue is read as a deliberate totality, not ornament, setting up the king's neglect
gains.b: the couplet's praise of complete delight is given a setting, kingship, where that completeness becomes a danger

links.note: Kural 901 says men who fix their desire on the wife miss life's fine fruit; 196 measures the king's wedded intimacy as greater than the sea, and the story goes on to make that desire lose him his realm.
links.teaches: The Kural's chapter on following the wife assumes a fault in the yielding; the epic gives a blameless, chaste queen (verse 7, வீடாத கற்பின்) and lawful marriage, and still the husband's boundless absorption alone ruins him, so the rule holds without any fault in the woman.

gains.a: the celebration of the wedding season acquires its moral edge from a stated rule
gains.b: the couplet's claim is tested on a case where the wife is beyond reproach, showing the danger lies in the man's desire, not in her

links.note: Verse 179 praises Vijayai's soles as if made without bone or sinew (என்பொடு நரம்பு இன்றி); Naladiyar 46 lists bone (என்பு) and sinew (நரம்பு) among the parts of the body and asks which of them is the garlanded woman.
links.teaches: Two Jain works use the same two words to opposite ends: the epic's praise must imagine the beloved's body without bone and sinew, while the quatrain dissolves her into them, so the courtly portrait depends on the very forgetting the ascetic verse is written to undo.

gains.a: the hyperbole of the boneless foot is seen to deny exactly what the renouncer insists on, showing what the praise leaves out
gains.b: the quatrain's list is shown answering a real literary convention of praise, not an abstract desire

links.note: Verse 192 praises Vijayai's red-cornered eyes as fighting carp (களிக் கயல் பொருவ); Naladiyar 44's renunciant refuses men who call eyes பொருகயல் and sees an eye as a scooped-out palm fruit.
links.teaches: The Naladiyar's renunciant names the epic's own stock of praise as the temptation he walks past, and the epic shows that praise doing its work on a king who does not walk past it.

gains.a: the stock carp-eye simile is shown to be a recognised snare in the ethical literature, not neutral ornament
gains.b: the quatrain's 'petty men' who praise eyes are given a full instance in a celebrated poem, and a consequence in the king's fall

links.note: 195 has the king linger with his wife as a monsoon cloud lingers; 198 says the king slipped from guarding the earth (மண் அகம் காவலின் வழுக்கி) while joined to her.
links.teaches: The lingering that the wedding verses present as pure delight is the same act that 198 names as a lapse in the king's guard, so the romantic sequence is already the first step of the political fall.

links.note: In 190 king and queen drink each other as nectar and wine; in 199 they drink the flood of love without pause while fortune slips from the king of the moon-white parasol.
links.teaches: The drinking image moves from mutual delight to unceasing consumption: what was a figure of shared love becomes the measure of the time in which the king's fortune leaks away.

links.note: 188 likens the wedded pair to the three-eyed god and his goddess joined; in 208 a counsellor cites the god's taking the mountain king's daughter into half his body as a great blame (பெரும் பழி).
links.teaches: The same divine union serves the narrator as the highest praise of the couple and the counsellor as a warning of shame from desire, so the epic lets its own simile be turned against the king within twenty verses.

links.note: 187 says the two were joined by the பான்மை for joining; 215 says the king followed the way of her mind because a former பான்மை (முனம் ஆகிய பான்மை) sprouted, ignoring all warning.
links.teaches: If பான்மை in 187 is read as destiny, the marriage and the king's ruinous absorption have one source in the epic's account, apportioned former deeds, while 187 also names the ministers' reasoning: fate and judgment are both given as causes.

links.note: 183 likens Vijayai in her father's palace to Tirumakal on the lotus; 232 has Tirumakal leave Sachchandan without a word, the king left alone.
links.teaches: The king wins a woman praised as the goddess of fortune and, through his absorption in her, loses the goddess of fortune herself: the epic turns its own epithet into the measure of the cost.

source_issues: 182 spells the queen's name விசயை; 201 spells it விசையை.
175 line 1 (பக்கத்தால் கவிழிய வாய் மேல் பிறங்காப் பாண்டிலா) and 176 line 3 (சேடு ஆவ நாழிகையின்) do not construe readily; possible corruption or word division problems.
189 line 4 (தீது இலார் திளைப்பின் ஆமான் செல்வமே) is obscure as divided.
